## Overview

Weeks 13 and 14 focus on genome assembly, annotation review, comparative analysis, and connecting genomic results back to phenotype.

## Purpose

- Evaluate DNA sequencing results and microbial genome assemblies.
- Submit an assembly job to BV-BRC.
- Apply bioinformatics tools to assemble genomes and analyze predicted coding sequences.

## Learning Outcomes

- Explain the purpose of the bioinformatics tools and workflows used.
- Discuss the significance of genome assembly.
- Practice using web-based bioinformatics tools.
- Explore genome assemblies and annotations.
- Describe the workflow for microbial genome assembly.
- Collect and interpret genomic data in the context of phenotypic analyses.
- Revise the draft for the individual and group projects.
- Explain how this work contributes to the overall experimental goal.

## Skills and Knowledge

### Skills

- Perform sequence-read quality review.
- Assemble microbial genomes.
- Annotate and explore genome content.

### Knowledge

- Steps required to assemble a microbial genome.
- Tools for filtering, assembly, annotation, and metabolic modeling.
- Cloud-based bioinformatics workflow submission.

## Task

Work in pairs to obtain, explore, and interpret genome data and then connect those results to the phenotypic evidence collected earlier in the course.

## Criteria for Success

Successful completion requires use of BV-BRC and SeqHub, careful documentation of outputs, and a complete ELN entry.

## Background

Students now use sequence data generated earlier in the course to compare isolates with *Delftia acidovorans* SPH-1 and other related genomes. The goal is to identify genetic features that explain the observed phenotype.

Figure @fig-module7-sequencing-overview is reused from the sequencing workflow to anchor where assembly, annotation, and comparative analysis fit into the broader pipeline.

## Procedures

### Lab Safety

This is a bioinformatics lab.

### Methods: Data Analysis

1. Create a free [BV-BRC.org](https://www.bv-brc.org/) account. Share your username with your instructors: [BV-BRC Usernames](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1lpaj0t5079yliPTzHsdgZJLTRco8sIU4es0Z-gK1eII/edit?usp=sharing). 
2. Access the sequences in our shared BV-BRC workspace.
3. Obtain concatenated sequences for your isolate from the shared workspace.
4. Follow the [Comprehensive Genome Analysis Service tutorial: Comprehensive Genome Analysis (CGA) Service | BV-BRC](https://www.bv-brc.org/docs/tutorial/comprehensive_genome_analysis/comprehensive_genome_analysis.html).
5. Start a job to assemble and annotate your genome by:

  i) Indicating the file(s) for your long-read Nanopore sequences (**single read**). If available, include the Nanopore data from each run.
  
  ii) Indicate the files for your paired Illumina sequences (**paired reads**). There should be R1 and R2 files for your isolate.
  
  iii) Leave the assembly parameters on **auto**.

6. Create an output folder in your BV-BRC workspace. Label the folder with your isolate’s name.
7. **Submit the job on [bv-brc.org](https://www.bv-brc.org/).** 
8. Wait… ~30 min to overnight, depending on server load and data used for assembly.
9. Create a free [SeqHub](https://seqhub.org/) account.
10. Upload the assembled genome FASTA file from [BV-BRC.org](https://www.bv-brc.org/) Comprehensive Genome Analysis Service to annotate and explore in SeqHub. 

### Methods: Genome Comparisons

1. Use BV-BRC to compare your genome to others in the database. For this, use the **Similar Genome Finder** tool. Review the [tutorial](https://www.bv-brc.org/docs/tutorial/similar_genome_finder/similar_genome_finder.html) for this workflow. 
2. Select your isolate’s genome.
3. Run the workflow and compare results using Reference and Representative Genomes and all Public Genomes.
4. Save your results and pie chart images. 
5. Record the similar genomes you identified:

::: {.callout-note}
Replace the note with your identified genomes.
:::

6. Use the Genome Alignment tool to compare your isolate’s genome to one or more similar genomes you identified in the previous step. Review the [tutorial](https://www.bv-brc.org/docs/tutorial/genome_alignment/genome_alignment.html) for this tool.

### Methods: Annotation Review and Genome Exploration

1. Use the results from the **BV-BRC Comprehensive Genome Analysis** service to review the annotation results.
2. Select the **annotation report** and review the findings.
3. Record the number of coding sequences (CDS) and other features found for your discussion. 
4. Record the top functional assignments of the genes identified. 

  i) What metabolic properties are most abundant? Record for your Discussion section.
  
  ii) How do these findings relate to your Biolog GEN III phenotypic data? Record for your Discussion section.
 
5. Review the CGA report and note whether plasmids or antibiotic resistance genes were identified.

### Methods: Genome Exploration with SeqHub

1. Create a free SeqHub account.
2. Review the features of this tool: [Documentation](https://seqhub.org/faq) & [Video](youtube.com/watch?v=H50FSLYy0CQ&feature=youtu.be) (7 min).
3. Find  the FASTA file for your genome in BV-BRC and download it.
4. Upload the FASTA file to SeqHub.
5. Explore the genome considering:

  i) Low-confidence annotations. What are they? Are they novel genes?
  
  ii) Hypothetical genes. What could they do? Are they similar to other sequences? 
  
  iii) Predicted Protein Interactions (PPI) tool. Are there protein interactions that are intriguing and could support your research question?
  
  iv) AI Agent. What questions can you ask the agent to learn about the genomic potential of your isolate?
  
  v) Protein Folding. Are there proteins of interest that could be folded?

6. Use the (AI) agent to help you understand and search for genes.
7. Which genes of interest did you identify? Why are they intriguing? Keep these answers in mind when writing your **discussion section**.

## Discussion 

- How did BV-BRC assemble your genome? How “good” was your assembly? 
Hint: review the Assembly results folder from BV-BRC and note the number of contigs, their sizes, and any other relevant information.

- What factors can affect the quality of the assembled genome? Compared to other isolates sequenced, is your genome larger? 

- Apart from research, what other applications are there for gene prediction and annotation? 

- What can the Predicted Protein Interactions (PPI) network contribute to your research? 

- Identify at least one change made to the lab protocol, whether intentional or accidental (e.g., wrong amount of reagent used, contamination, etc). How did, or could, this change/accident impact your final results?
